newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Group plans pepper futures exchange.
newsitem.headline: Group plans pepper futures exchange.

text.p: Aiming to bring more order to the global market for pepper and other spices, the International Spice Group plans to launch a pepper futures exchange, the first of its kind for spices, an official said Tuesday.

The exchange, to be set up in January in Cochin in southern India, will help hedge options for traders of pepper, the most widely used spice, said Fazli Husain, senior commodity marketing officer of the U.N.-backed International Trade Centre.
He said the new exchange would make the international pepper market less volatile.
Black pepper, which accounts for about 30 percent of all spices traded in the world, determines the value of the global spice market, which was around $2 billion last year.
"In the early part of this decade when the price of pepper was low, the spice market was less than $1.5 billion. The market is at today's high levels because of high pepper prices," he said.
The spice group was set up in the late 1970s and supported by the Commonwealth Secretariat and the International Trade Centre. It aims to help spice-producing countries achieve sustainable growth.
Husain was among some 40 overseas delegates at a symposium in Colombo this week to discuss ways to boost spice exports.
India is the world's biggest spice exporter, having produced one-quarter of the 450,000 tons of spices sold in the international market last year, he said.
With the exception of Brazil, the most important spice producing nations are in Asia, with India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam the most prolific producers.
The United States, the largest market for spices, imported 262,743 metric tons worth $445.3 million in 1995 and European Union countries imported 195,801 tons worth $444.4 million.
Husain said the main concern for the importing countries is the quality. "Not one exporting country can claim at this stage that they are giving a clean and quality product," he said.
Most complaints involve pesticide residue in spices, since developing countries tend to overuse pesticides to maximize production, Husain said.
Among the principal spices traded globally are pepper, paprika, cinnamon, cloves, ginger, tumeric and nutmeg.
"It is a growth market," Husain said. "For as long as people continue to appreciate food, there will be a growing demand for spices."
